lead: A waveguide tee is a three-port junction: a branch guide joined to the side of a through guide, splitting power from one guide into two or combining two into one. A branch on the broad wall makes an E-plane tee, on the narrow wall an H-plane tee. A magic tee puts both on one junction and becomes a matched four-port with two isolated pairs of arms. Tees feed antenna pairs, balanced mixers, radar comparators and tuners.
prereq: You need: the TE₁₀ mode of a rectangular guide (see Rectangular and circular waveguides: TE and TM modes) and the S-matrix tests in S-parameters and the scattering matrix.

blocks.text: Ports 1 and 2 are the ends of the through (collinear) guide and port 3 is the branch. In the TE₁₀ mode E runs across the narrow dimension b; the broad wall has width a.

items: E-plane tee (series tee): the branch is joined to the broad wall, so its axis lies in the plane of E. A wave fed into port 3 leaves ports 1 and 2 with equal power and 180° apart, because the E-field lines turn opposite ways into the two arms. Seen from the branch, the two arms are in series.

H-plane tee (shunt tee): the branch is joined to the narrow wall, so its axis lies in the plane of the magnetic field H. A wave fed into port 3 leaves ports 1 and 2 with equal power and in phase. Seen from the branch, the arms are in parallel.

blocks.text: With the branch matched (S₃₃ = 0), the usual matrices are

blocks.where: rows and columns are ports 1, 2, 3. The signs of S₁₃ and S₂₃ carry the in-phase (H) or opposite (E) split. Both matrices are symmetric (reciprocal) and every column has |S₁ⱼ|² + |S₂ⱼ|² + |S₃ⱼ|² = ¼ + ¼ + ½ = 1 (lossless).

blocks.text: S₁₁ = S₂₂ = ½: a collinear port reflects a quarter of the power fed into it. No three-port tee can do better, as the next section shows.

sections.h3: Why a three-port tee cannot be matched

blocks.text: Suppose a lossless reciprocal three-port were matched: S₁₁ = S₂₂ = S₃₃ = 0. Apply S†S = I.

items: Add the three and halve: |S₁₂|² + |S₁₃|² + |S₂₃|² = 3/2. Subtract each equation in turn: |S₁₂|² = |S₁₃|² = |S₂₃|² = ½, so none of the three can be zero.
Columns 1 and 2 must be orthogonal: S₁₁S*₁₂ + S₂₁S*₂₂ + S₃₁S*₃₂ = 0. With S₁₁ = S₂₂ = 0 this leaves S₃₁S*₃₂ = S₁₃S*₂₃ = 0.
A product of two numbers of magnitude 1/√2 cannot be zero. The assumption is false: a lossless reciprocal three-port cannot be matched at every port.

blocks.text: So a real tee always reflects at some port. Two ways round this are used: add a fourth port (the magic tee and the couplers of Directional couplers and hybrid rings) or accept loss (the Wilkinson divider of Power dividers and attenuators).

A magic tee (hybrid tee) is an E-plane and an H-plane branch on the same junction. Ports 1 and 2 are collinear, port 3 is the H-arm and port 4 is the E-arm. Matching posts or irises inside the junction make all four ports matched; the geometry then gives the rest.

items: Power into the H-arm splits equally and in phase to ports 1 and 2; none reaches the E-arm (S₄₃ = 0).

Power into the E-arm splits equally and 180° apart to ports 1 and 2; none reaches the H-arm. The E-arm field is odd about the centre plane of the junction, the H-arm field is even, so they cannot couple.
Ports 1 and 2 are isolated from each other (S₁₂ = 0).
Waves fed into ports 1 and 2 together: their sum leaves the H-arm and their difference leaves the E-arm. For this reason the H-arm is called the sum (Σ) port and the E-arm the difference (Δ) port.

blocks.where: rows and columns are ports 1, 2, 3 (H), 4 (E). Check: symmetric, so reciprocal; each column has two entries of magnitude 1/√2, so Σ|Sᵢⱼ|² = 1; columns 1 and 2 give ½ − ½ = 0, so they are orthogonal. The matrix is unitary and matched.

blocks.text: Some syllabi list corners, bends and twists with tees, because tee arms reach their loads through them. A mitred corner or a smooth E-plane or H-plane bend turns a guide by 90° with little reflection; a twist rotates the cross-section, so an arm can feed a guide whose broad wall faces the other way. An E-H tuner is a magic tee with sliding shorts in the E- and H-arms, used to match an unknown load.

examples.question: An ideal H-plane tee (S-matrix above) has 10 mW fed into collinear port 1, with ports 2 and 3 ended in matched loads. Find the power reflected at port 1, the power at ports 2 and 3, and the input VSWR at port 1.
steps: The incident wave is a₁ = √10 mW<sup>½</sup> = 3.162; a₂ = a₃ = 0.
Outgoing waves are column 1 of S times a₁: b₁ = ½ × 3.162 = 1.581, b₂ = −½ × 3.162 = −1.581, b₃ = (1/√2) × 3.162 = 2.236.
Powers: P₁(reflected) = 1.581² = 2.5 mW, P₂ = 2.5 mW, P₃ = 2.236² = 5.0 mW.
Balance: 2.5 + 2.5 + 5.0 = 10.0 mW, so the tee is lossless as its matrix says.
Input VSWR at port 1: |S₁₁| = 0.5, so VSWR = (1 + 0.5)/(1 − 0.5) = 3.0. Return loss = −20 log₁₀ 0.5 = 6.02 dB.
examples.answer: 2.5 mW reflects at port 1, 2.5 mW leaves port 2, 5 mW leaves the branch; the input VSWR is 3.0. Only the branch is matched, as the three-port proof requires.
examples.check:
import numpy as np
r=2**-0.5
H=np.array([[.5,-.5,r],[-.5,.5,r],[r,r,0]])
b=H@np.array([10**0.5,0,0])
print(np.round(b**2,2))

examples.question: Two in-phase signals of 8 W and 2 W are fed into ports 1 and 2 of an ideal magic tee; ports 3 (H) and 4 (E) are matched. Find the power leaving the H-arm and the E-arm. Repeat when the 2 W signal is 180° out of phase.
steps: Wave amplitudes: a₁ = √8 = 2.828 W<sup>½</sup>, a₂ = √2 = 1.414 W<sup>½</sup>.
Rows 1 and 2 have zeros in columns 1 and 2, so b₁ = b₂ = 0: nothing reflects. Total out = 9 + 1 = 10 W, equal to the input.
With a₂ = −1.414 (180°): b₃ = (2.828 − 1.414)/1.414 = 1.0 → P₃ = 1 W, and b₄ = (2.828 + 1.414)/1.414 = 3.0 → P₄ = 9 W. The sum and difference ports swap roles.
examples.answer: In phase: 9 W from the H-arm and 1 W from the E-arm. Antiphase: 1 W from the H-arm and 9 W from the E-arm. Equal in-phase inputs would give all the power at the H-arm and none at the E-arm.

traps: Swapping the arms. The H-arm (narrow-wall branch) gives the in-phase split; the E-arm (broad-wall branch) gives the 180° split.
Writing a fully matched lossless three-port tee. It cannot exist; an ideal tee has S₁₁ = S₂₂ = ½.
Adding powers instead of waves. With 8 W and 2 W in phase, the H-arm gives (√8 + √2)²/2 = 9 W, not 10 W; the other 1 W leaves the E-arm.
Renumbering ports in the middle of an answer. Keep 1 and 2 collinear, 3 the H-arm and 4 the E-arm, or the signs in the matrix change.

quiz.q: Which wall carries the branch of an E-plane tee, and how are its collinear outputs phased when it is fed from the branch?
quiz.a: The broad wall, so the branch axis lies in the plane of E. Ports 1 and 2 leave with equal power, 180° apart.

quiz.q: State the two isolation conditions of an ideal magic tee.
quiz.a: S₃₄ = S₄₃ = 0 between the H-arm and the E-arm, and S₁₂ = S₂₁ = 0 between the two collinear arms.

quiz.q: Write the S-matrix of an ideal magic tee (port 3 H-arm, port 4 E-arm) and show that it is unitary.
quiz.a: S = (1/√2)[0 0 1 1; 0 0 1 −1; 1 1 0 0; 1 −1 0 0]. Each column has two entries of magnitude 1/√2, so Σ|Sᵢⱼ|² = ½ + ½ = 1. Columns 1 and 2: (1·1 + 1·(−1))/2 = 0; columns 3 and 4 likewise give 0; other pairs share no non-zero row. So S†S = I.

quiz.q: An ideal magic tee has 4 W fed into its E-arm. Find the power at ports 1, 2 and 3 and the phase between ports 1 and 2.
quiz.a: Column 4 of S: b₁ = +2/√2, b₂ = −2/√2 (a₄ = 2 W<sup>½</sup>), so P₁ = P₂ = 2 W, 180° apart. S₃₄ = 0, so P₃ = 0.

quiz.q: A real magic tee reflects 4 % of the power at each collinear port and has 0.3 dB loss. Which properties of the ideal matrix fail, and how is the tee corrected?
quiz.a: |S₁₁| = |S₂₂| = √0.04 = 0.2, so the diagonal is no longer zero (return loss 14 dB); the loss makes each column sum about 10<sup>−0.03</sup> = 0.933 instead of 1, so S is not unitary. A matching post and iris inside the junction (or tuning screws) bring the reflections down over the band; the matrix of the real tee is measured with a network analyser.

quiz.q: Two equal in-phase signals feed ports 1 and 2 of a magic tee. Why does the E-arm receive nothing, and what changes if one signal shifts by 90°?
quiz.a: The E-arm output is (a₁ − a₂)/√2, which is zero for equal in-phase waves. With a 90° shift, a₂ = ja₁: |b₄|² = |a₁|²|1 − j|²/2 = |a₁|², so the E- and H-arms each get half the total power.

beyond: The magic-tee behaviour is now often printed as a microstrip rat-race or built in substrate-integrated waveguide. Monopulse radar comparators use four magic tees to form sum and difference beams. Search for "monopulse comparator" and "orthomode transducer".
